title: The First Patient at Panzi Hospital Had Not Come to Give Birth
dek: In 1999 Denis Mukwege opened two rooms in Bukavu for mothers, and the women who arrived changed what the hospital became.

story.event: Opening a maternity hospital in Bukavu and turning it to the care of survivors of sexual violence
story.summary: In 1999 Denis Mukwege, a gynaecologist whose hospital at Lemera had been attacked in October 1996, opened Panzi Hospital in Bukavu as a small clinic meant for deliveries and caesareans. Its first patient was a survivor of rape; as many more arrived, he devoted himself to treating survivors of sexual violence, and the hospital added psychological, economic and legal support. He shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize with Nadia Murad.
paragraphs: On the night of 6 October 1996, rebels attacked the hospital at Lemera in South Kivu, where Denis Mukwege was the gynaecologist and medical director. In his Nobel lecture he said more than thirty people were killed, patients in their beds and staff who could not escape; the Panzi Foundation puts it at nearly forty. He had trained in France because he had seen women at Lemera live with lasting injuries from childbirth. "It took me two years before I felt I could be useful again," he later told UN News.

He went home to Bukavu, and in 1999 he opened Panzi Hospital on an empty plot in a poor, hilly district on the city's edge, with help from international aid organisations. He meant it for mothers. Congo's maternal death rate was among the highest in the world, which he called unbearable, and NPR reported that about one woman in a hundred in Bukavu died in childbirth. At first, he said in a 2014 oral history interview, there were just two rooms, where he expected to do deliveries and caesarean sections.

But the region was at war, and the first patient admitted had not come to give birth. She had been raped and shot. He later said he took it for a lone act. Within about six months, he told UN News, many more women were arriving with almost the same account. According to the biography published by the Nobel Foundation, he was then the only obstetrician-gynaecologist in the region. He decided to devote himself to repairing the injuries of women who had survived sexual violence, a choice that would later put his own life and family in danger.

Surgery alone was not enough. Some women whose wounds had been treated were losing the will to live, he said, so the hospital hired psychologists and social workers, then worked with other groups on economic support and opened a legal clinic so that survivors could seek justice. NPR counted 45,482 survivors treated between 1999 and 2015; the Panzi Foundation now gives more than 91,000 across all its programmes. The hospital still delivers babies. In 2018 Mukwege shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Nadia Murad. "You can't operate against violence," he has said. "You can only abolish it."

quote.text: If he be compassionate towards the afflictions of others, it shows that his heart is like the noble tree, that is wounded itself, when it gives the balm.
quote.locator: Essay XIII, "Of Goodness and Goodness of Nature"
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon's tree gives its balm only by being cut. Mukwege's story holds both halves: a surgeon who needed two years to feel useful after Lemera, who then chose work that brought him daily to other people's deepest injuries, and who later put his own safety at risk for it.

reflection: Mukwege did not plan the work he became known for. He built two rooms for mothers, and the patients who came showed him what the hospital had to become. He kept the maternity ward and took on the rest. Notice, too, the two years before it: a surgeon who needed time before he felt he could be useful again, and who said so.

You carry responsibility for things that are not finished, and some days the weight of it is heavier than the work in front of you. Bacon's tree is not told to stop giving balm. It is only honest that the giving has a cost. Saying so, to yourself or to someone you trust, is part of keeping the work going.
invitation: Today, tell one person you trust about one part of your work that has been costing you more than you have admitted. You do not need to solve it; only name it out loud.

The first patient was a survivor of rape, not a woman in labour, and Mukwege at first took it for an isolated case
The Lemera hospital was attacked on 6 October 1996 and patients and staff were killed (more than thirty, or nearly forty)

research_notes: Lemera death toll: Mukwege's Nobel lecture (2018) says more than thirty people were killed; the Panzi Foundation's October 2026 press release says nearly 40; UN News (2016) says all his patients had been murdered. The story gives the first two with attribution. Leaving Lemera: the English text of the Nobel lecture reads 'Forced to leave Lemera in 1999, we set up the Panzi hospital', while Right Livelihood says Lemera was destroyed in 1996 and UN News says that, unable to continue at Lemera, he returned to Bukavu and founded Panzi in 1999; the story does not date his departure from Lemera. Right Livelihood places the founding directly after 1996 and dates the new violence 'from 1999'; the Nobel biography, the WHO, NPR, UN News and Mukwege's 2014 oral history all give 1999 for the founding, which the story uses. The Nobel biography says war 'broke out shortly after' the founding, but the Second Congo War began in 1998; the story follows Mukwege's own phrase that 'we were in the midst of a conflict'. Numbers treated differ by date and by counting: UN News (2016) more than 40,000; NPR (2016) 45,482 between 1999 and 2015; Nobel biography and Right Livelihood more than 50,000; Panzi Foundation (2026) over 91,000 'across all programs'. The story gives NPR's dated figure and the foundation's current figure, attributed. The 'six months' comes from Mukwege's own words to UN News. Right Livelihood wrongly dates the Nobel Prize to 2019; the Nobel Foundation and WHO give 2018. The 2014 oral history is translated from French and appears identically on the Council on Foreign Relations site (https://www.cfr.org/blog/champions-change-dr-denis-mukwege); the Georgetown copy is cited. Graphic details in the sources are left out deliberately. The Bacon passage lists signs of a good nature; it is applied by analogy to the cost of care.
